volumes.title: Five Sets of Initials
volumes.text:
I am Barnaby Thresh, joiner, of Cooper’s Row in Emberwick, and these are notes kept at my bench in a slow January. The bench is older than I am by a good deal. It is beech, black with handling, and it has stood under this window through four joiners before me.

Crouch down and look beneath the front rail and you will find us all. H.T., who built it. M.T., his daughter Martha. J.O., who was no relation and the best of us. R.T., my father. Then B.T., cut by me at nineteen with more flourish than skill.

There is room to the right of mine for one more set, perhaps two. I am sixty-seven, with no child and no apprentice. I mention it only because the bench is a thing I look at all day, and the gap has begun to look back.

volumes.title: The Carter’s Daughter
volumes.text:
Notes at the bench, Cooper’s Row, February. Dunstan Addle the carter came in on Tuesday with a load of oak and a daughter. The oak I had ordered. The daughter is Wren, fourteen, who he says is no use with horses because she will stop to look at gateposts. He asked would I, Barnaby Thresh, try her till midsummer. I said the bench had seen worse, which is not certain.

I gave her a saw, a board and a pencilled line. Her cut set off well, lost heart, and wandered away to the left like the Ember going through the Lowlands. She looked at it for some time. Then she asked for another board, without being told.

I have set her to sweeping and to learning the names of things. She sweeps badly. She learns names as if she were collecting them.

volumes.title: A Door for the Bakery
volumes.text:
Barnaby Thresh, joiner, at his bench. This fortnight’s work is a new street door for Mrs. Quince’s bakery in Oven Lane, the old one having swollen and stuck so often that customers took to knocking on the window with pennies.

It is oak, framed and boarded, and heavy enough to need the two of us to turn it over. My apprentice Wren Addle has been six weeks with me. She cannot yet saw to a line, but I find she can read a board. She ran her thumb down one and said the grain turned back on itself near the end, and it did. Nobody taught her that. I only learned it at thirty.

We hung the door on Friday. It closes with one finger and a sound like a book shutting. Mrs. Quince paid in coin and a warm loaf, and Wren carried the loaf.

volumes.title: The Cradle Rockers
volumes.text:
A cradle this month, for the miller’s first child, due with the lambs. I am Barnaby Thresh, joiner of Emberwick, and I have made some forty cradles on this old beech bench. My father made mine on it, and I am told I complained of the workmanship from the first night.

The rockers are the particular part. Too flat and the child is merely in a box. Too round and it goes over like a herring boat. You find the curve by eye, and by rocking the thing empty with one finger until it settles the way a breath does.

Wren Addle, my apprentice since February, cut the joints for the foot end. Three I recut. The fourth went together with a push and stayed. She said nothing at all, and swept the entire shop without being asked, corners included.

volumes.title: Sharpening Day
volumes.text:
It rained on Emberwick from Monday to Thursday, so we sharpened. A joiner’s shop is half edges, and I, Barnaby Thresh, have let mine go this spring, for a reason I shall come to.

Wren Addle, the apprentice, had every chisel and plane iron out along the bench in order of size, like a choir. She worked the stones the whole of Tuesday. I showed her once how a good edge refuses to catch the light, and by afternoon she was holding irons up to the window and frowning like a jeweller.

The reason is my hands. In wet weather the knuckles swell and the fine grip goes. I note it here as I would note a split in a board: a fact about the material, to be worked around. Wren sharpened mine too. They have not been so keen since my father had the doing of them.

volumes.title: The Library Window
volumes.text:
Notes at the joiner’s bench, Cooper’s Row, midsummer. The north window of Emberwick Library has let in the rain since before I was apprenticed, and this month the librarian sent for me to make a new sash. I am Barnaby Thresh. I have wanted that job for forty years.

The frame is plain work. The glazing bars are not: thin as reeds, each with its little moulding, meeting in joints you could hide under a thumbnail. My hands would not hold steady for them. So Wren Addle cut them, my apprentice of five months, with me on a box beside her saying less and less.

Eleven bars, and I could fault two. The window went in on Saturday. The librarian paid fairly and added that we might each keep our books a month past the date. Wren asked if the offer could be had in writing.

volumes.title: Elm for the Ferry Steps
volumes.text:
I am Barnaby Thresh, joiner, and for nine days I have been away from my bench, which does not suit me. The landing steps at the Ember ferry had rotted, and the ferryman wanted new ones in elm, since elm will sit in water for a lifetime and only grow more stubborn.

We worked on the bank, my apprentice Wren Addle and I, with the boards across two trestles and the river going by at our elbows. Nothing was level. The wind turned over my drawings. Wren went in to the knee twice and to the waist once, and came out holding the mallet above her head like a prize.

The steps are sound and the ferryman is pleased. But I missed the bench as you miss a table at dinnertime. I had not known how much of my straightness I borrow from it.

volumes.title: A Mistake in Ash
volumes.text:
A bad Thursday at the bench in Cooper’s Row. We are making a long ladder in ash for the bell-ringers, and my apprentice Wren Addle cut the last pair of joints on the wrong side of her line. A whole pole wasted, and clean ash is not had every week.

She put down the saw and went to fetch her coat. I am Barnaby Thresh, fifty years a joiner, and I knew that walk. So I pulled open the bench drawer, the deep one, and took out a small oak wedge, cut badly crooked, with B.T. on it in my father’s pencil.

Every joiner at this bench has had a first real mistake kept in that drawer. There are five. Martha’s is a door peg. I wrote W.A. on the spoiled end of the ash and put it in with the others. Wren hung her coat up again.

volumes.title: The Hollow in the Top
volumes.text:
There is a hollow in the top of my bench, just left of the vice, where every joiner who has owned it stood to plane. You can lay a straight edge across and slide a penny under. My father meant to flatten it. So did Martha Thresh before him, by all accounts. I, Barnaby Thresh, have meant to since I was thirty.

This week, with the autumn orders not yet in, I sharpened the long plane and set to. I took three shavings. Then my apprentice Wren Addle, who has been with me since February, asked what I would rest small work in afterwards. I had no answer. Half of what I make sits in that hollow to be held.

I oiled the three pale stripes until they darkened. The bench is not flat. It is the shape of the work done on it, and I shall leave it so.

volumes.title: Table for the Lantern Inn
volumes.text:
The Lantern Inn on the Grey Coast ordered a table to seat twenty fishermen, and my shop in Cooper’s Row is not the length of twenty fishermen. I am Barnaby Thresh, joiner. We built it with the street door open and one end out in the Row, so that for a week the whole of Emberwick stepped round our work and gave an opinion on it.

The opinions I leave out. The joints are Wren Addle’s. She is my apprentice, nine months at the bench, and she cut all eight where the legs meet the frame while I held the lamp and kept my swollen hands in my apron. They went home with a knock of the mallet apiece.

The baker’s boy asked who made it. I said, “The shop did.” Wren looked up, then went on planing. A shop, I notice, has become two people.

volumes.title: A Stool by the Stove
volumes.text:
December, Cooper’s Row. I have made myself a stool. It is the first thing I have built for my own use since my tool chest, and it stands by the stove, where a joiner with winter hands can be warm and still see the bench. I am Barnaby Thresh, and I find I can direct a good deal of work from a seated position.

Wren Addle now takes the orders at the door. She came in February on trial till midsummer, and midsummer passed without either of us mentioning it. Yesterday she mentioned it. She asked whether she was to stay.

I handed her a board with a pencilled line, as on her first morning, and she sawed it. I laid the rule against the cut and no light came through. I said the bench had waited some time for someone who could do that.

volumes.title: The Sixth Set
volumes.text:
The last of these notes, written from the stool by the stove on the shortest day. I am Barnaby Thresh, joiner of Emberwick, and this morning I gave my apprentice Wren Addle the small gouge my father gave me, and told her where to kneel.

Under the front rail of the bench are five sets of initials, from old H.T. who built it down to my own. It took her an hour. She cut W.A. to the right of B.T., plainly, with none of the flourish I wasted on mine. There is room beyond hers for one more.

The bench is hers when I am done with it, and I am in no hurry. She is planing as I write, standing in the hollow where we have all stood. These pages go in the deep drawer with the six mistakes, for whoever comes seventh.

volumes.title: On Wobbles
volumes.text:
Every chair has a trouble. I say so as Jessamy Poole, chair-mender, of Rushbottom Lane in Emberwick, who has mended some four thousand chairs in thirty years and never yet made one. This book sets the troubles down in order, beginning with the commonest.

A wobble is rarely what you think. Miss Garnet, the schoolmistress, brought me a chair that rocked corner to corner. She had already trimmed one leg herself, then another to match, and was on her way to owning a footstool. I set the chair on my flat stone. It stood like a judge. The trouble was her schoolroom floor.

So look under the chair before you look at it. I tell everyone that, from my seat by the shop window, beside a ladder-back armchair with ticket forty-one tied to its arm. That one is not mine. It is waiting to be collected.

volumes.title: On Creaks
volumes.text:
A creak is a joint talking. Somewhere two pieces of wood that were once tight have come loose enough to rub, and the chair is letting you know. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Emberwick, and I can generally silence one in an afternoon with glue, a wedge and patience.

Generally. The widow Pargeter of Tanner’s Yard sent down her rocking chair with a split arm and a note pinned to the seat. Mend the arm, it said. Touch the creak and I shall know. Her husband had sat in that rocker forty winters, and the creak on the backward swing was the sound of him thinking.

I mended the arm. I left the creak exactly where it was, and tested it twice to be certain. It is the only time I have charged a customer for a thing I did not do, and she paid it gladly.

volumes.title: On Loose Rungs
volumes.text:
The rungs of a chair are the rails that run between its legs, low down, and they come loose for one reason. Somebody tips back. I am Jessamy Poole, who mends chairs in Rushbottom Lane, and I could keep my shop on that habit alone.

Mr. Brill of the Lantern Inn sends me fourteen chairs every spring. They arrive on a cart, loose as a bag of kindling, having spent the winter under fishermen who tell long stories on two legs. I knock each one apart, clean the old glue from the sockets, and put it together again tighter than it was born.

I have told Mr. Brill his customers might try sitting on all four legs. He says a man cannot describe the size of a fish that way. So the cart comes each April, and I am not, truthfully, sorry to see it.

volumes.title: On Sagging Seats
volumes.text:
A rush seat lasts twenty years and then lets you down slowly, which is kinder than most things. You notice one evening that you are sitting in the chair rather than on it. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender, of Emberwick, and I have rewoven more seats than I have had hot dinners, since a seat once started cannot be left.

The rush comes off the marsh in high summer. I cut it myself, dry it in the loft till it smells of hay and river, then damp it and twist it as I weave, round and round the frame until the four sides meet in the middle like the back of an envelope.

The best seat I ever wove is on the ladder-back armchair in my window, ticket forty-one. A young seaman named Ned Harrow left it and said he would be back by spring. That was eleven springs ago.

volumes.title: On Woodworm
volumes.text:
You will know woodworm by its holes, small and round as if someone had gone over the chair with a pin, and by the pale dust beneath it of a morning. It is the one trouble I, Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Rushbottom Lane, cannot always mend, and a mender should say so plainly.

The verger of Emberwick brought me the old vestry chair, in which six generations of clergy had sat to pull on their boots. I pressed my thumb to the back leg and it went in as a thumb goes into cake. I told him the chair was finished. He took it well, for a verger.

But one spindle of the back was sound, dark and hard as horn. I kept it. A year later it went into a farmhouse chair from the Northern Fells, where it will do another century. Chairs have heirs, if you arrange it.

volumes.title: On Too Much Paint
volumes.text:
Some chairs suffer from kindness. Every few years someone gives them a fresh coat, until the turnings fill up and the chair looks made of dough. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender, and scraping such a chair is the nearest my trade comes to reading.

The Doble family’s kitchen chair came to my shop in Rushbottom Lane wearing seven coats. Under the cream was a green, under the green a blue from old Mrs. Doble’s day, then a brown, a red, and a yellow nobody living would own to. At the bottom, on bare elm, I found two pencilled words in a child’s large letters: Hetty’s chair.

I left that corner unscraped and waxed over it. I did my thinking about it in the evening, in the armchair by my window. It has ticket forty-one on its arm and is not mine to sit in. I sit in it regardless.

volumes.title: On Grand Chairs
volumes.text:
A grand chair is built to be looked at, and it is a mistake to ask more of it. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Emberwick, and the grandest I ever handled was the Mayor’s chair from the Moot Hall: oak, carved with herons and wheat-sheaves, and gilded wherever gilt would stick.

Mrs. Oldacre, the Mayor, had it carried to my shop by four men. Nothing was broken. Its trouble, she said, was that no mayor in a hundred years had sat in it for an hour without thinking of resigning. The seat was flat as a doorstep and the back stood bolt upright.

I eased the back a little, hollowed the seat a little more, and hid a cushion under the velvet. Council meetings now run forty minutes longer. Mrs. Oldacre says the town has not thanked me, and she is not sure she does.

volumes.title: On Broken Backs
volumes.text:
When the back of a chair breaks there is always a story, and it is usually laughter. Mr. Hogg, the Emberwick blacksmith, leaned back at his own table to enjoy a joke about a goose, and the top rail parted with a crack they heard in the street. He brought me the pieces in his apron. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender, and I asked for the joke as well.

A break like that I mend by letting in new wood, shaped to fit the old and pinned so the two grip one another. It takes a day. The joint ends up stronger than the rail around it.

It also shows. I will stain a mend but never hide one. Mr. Hogg’s chair has a pale stripe across its shoulders, and he tells me he points it out to visitors, and then tells the joke again.

volumes.title: On High Chairs
volumes.text:
A child’s high chair has troubles of its own, most of them sticky. I am Jessamy Poole, who mends chairs in Rushbottom Lane, Emberwick, and I see the Tunney family’s high chair about once in three years, between babies.

It is ash, tall and narrow, with a little tray on a wooden catch. Nine Tunneys have sat in it. The catch wears out because each child discovers, at about ten months, that the tray will come off if hammered with a spoon. I have made that catch four times and now cut two at once.

Along the front rail there is a row of small tooth marks, some shallow, some very determined. Mrs. Tunney asked once if I could sand them out. I said I could, and didn’t. She can tell you which marks are whose. The deep ones, she says, belong to the quietest child.

volumes.title: On Chairs Nobody Sits In
volumes.text:
You would suppose that the safest chair is the one nobody uses. It is the opposite. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Emberwick, and half the chairs brought to me from best parlours have simply dried out and come apart from loneliness, like a boat left on the shingle.

A chair needs sitting in. Weight keeps the joints snug, warmth keeps the wood from shrinking, and the daily shifting about is a sort of exercise. Miss Larch of Bell Street kept six good chairs under dust sheets for her visitors. When visitors finally came, two chairs sat down with them.

Which brings me to a confession. The ladder-back armchair in my window, ticket forty-one, has been sound these eleven years because I sit in it every evening. Its owner, a seaman called Ned Harrow, never came back for it. I call this maintenance. I have not charged for it.

volumes.title: On Stools
volumes.text:
The stool is the one seat with almost no troubles. Three legs will stand steady on any floor in the Lowlands, as every milkmaid knows, and there is no back to break and no arm to split. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Rushbottom Lane, and I have had perhaps five stools to mend in thirty years. A trade could starve on them.

I have been thinking about stools because I have been thinking about making. I have mended four thousand seats and never built one from the tree. A mender only ever meets a chair in the middle of its life.

And a letter came on Tuesday, from the Grey Coast, in a hand I did not know. Ned Harrow is ashore for good, it says, and begs to ask whether a certain armchair, left with me eleven years ago, is by any chance still about.

volumes.title: On Collecting Your Chair
volumes.text:
Ned Harrow came for his chair on a Saturday, eleven years late and grey in the beard. I am Jessamy Poole, chair-mender of Emberwick, and I untied ticket forty-one from the arm of the ladder-back in my window and stood aside.

He sat. He shifted. He stood up again and looked at the seat, and then at me. A rush seat takes the shape of whoever uses it, and that one had had eleven years of my evenings. “She’s sat to you now,” he said, quite kindly. He paid the old bill, which was ninepence, and would not take the chair.

Instead he ordered a new one, made for him from the start. So there is ash drying in my loft, and for the first time in thirty years I am at the beginning of a chair. Its trouble, when it comes, will at least be my own doing.

volumes.title: January: The Salt Box
volumes.text:
January. I am Tansy Wickett, I am eleven, and I have come to live for a year with my great-aunt Lovage, who makes boxes in Thimble Yard in Emberwick. My Da is mate of the ketch Curlew and sailed north on New Year’s Day. He will be gone until winter comes round again.

Aunt Lovage has a rule for me. One small box every month, each one given away when it is done. She says twelve boxes will teach me more than a hundred lectures, and that she does not know a hundred lectures anyway.

January’s is a salt box in pine, with a sloping lid, for her own kitchen. I sawed, I planed, I nailed. The lid sits up at one corner like a raised eyebrow. I said it was ruined. Aunt Lovage filled it with salt, hung it by the stove and said, “It holds salt. Box.”

volumes.title: February: The Seed Box
volumes.text:
February. Box two is for Mr. Fenn, who has the allotment behind the tannery and keeps his seeds in old socks. I am Tansy Wickett, and I am learning box-making from my great-aunt Lovage in Thimble Yard, one box a month.

A seed box wants little rooms inside, one for each kind. I cut the dividers to fit and they did not fit. I cut them again and they fitted somewhere else. Aunt Lovage says wood is not being awkward, it is only being exact, and that I am invited to join it. I got them in on the fourth try and wrote on each in pencil: peas, beans, marigold, and one marked Mystery.

A letter came from Da on the Curlew! They are past the Grey Coast and the cook has burnt the porridge twice. Mr. Fenn says the Mystery room is the one he will fill first.

volumes.title: March: The Button Box
volumes.text:
March, and a button box for Miss Odell the dressmaker, whose buttons live loose in a drawer and escape. I am Tansy Wickett, eleven, staying this year with my great-aunt Lovage the box-maker while my Da is at sea.

This box has a lid that slides in a groove. Aunt Lovage let me use the little grooving plane, which sings when it is going well. Mine sang, and then I made the lid too thin, so that when Miss Odell tipped the box to admire it the lid shot out and so did two hundred buttons. We hunted them for an hour. One was in the cat’s dish.

I made a second lid on Saturday. It slides if you ask it and stays if you don’t. Miss Odell gave me a button shaped like an anchor, to sew inside my coat for Da’s luck.

volumes.title: April: The Nesting Box
volumes.text:
April. I asked my great-aunt Lovage whether a bird box counts as a box, and she said anything with six sides and a reason counts. So this month’s is for the blue tits in the pear tree in Thimble Yard. I am Tansy Wickett, making one box a month for a year.

It is rough larch, because birds dislike a planed wall, and the roof leans so the rain runs off. Aunt Lovage bored the round door with a tool like a giant corkscrew, and I smoothed its edge with sandpaper wrapped round my thumb so nobody would catch a feather.

Then nothing happened for nine days. I watched from the window until Aunt said I was wearing a hole in the glass. On the tenth day a tit went in with moss. They are the worst customers we have had. They have not paid, and they complain constantly.

volumes.title: May: The Tea Caddy
volumes.text:
May. This is the first box I am not ashamed of. I am Tansy Wickett, and since January I have made a box a month in my great-aunt Lovage’s workshop, and given each away. This one is for the librarian at Emberwick Library, who keeps her tea in a paper bag.

It is cherry, my first hard wood, which smells faintly of almonds when you saw it. The corners are mitred, meaning each side leans in to meet the next like heads over a map, and inside there is a second lid to keep the air out.

When you lower the top it sinks the last little way by itself, with a sigh. Aunt Lovage closed it four times and said nothing, which from her is a speech. Da’s letter came the same day. The Curlew has seen ice, floating, the colour of the inside of a shell.

volumes.title: June: The Fly Box
volumes.text:
June. No letter from Da this month. I am Tansy Wickett, living this year with my great-aunt Lovage, the box-maker of Thimble Yard, while his ship the Curlew trades in the far north. A letter most months since January, and now none.

Aunt Lovage did not say he would be all right. She gave me a piece of pear wood no bigger than a slice of bread and told me old Tolly the ferryman needed a box for his fishing flies, to fit a waistcoat pocket. It has tiny brass hinges, let in flush, and a lining of cork. It took every afternoon I had.

That, I see now, was the idea. Tolly opened and shut it by the Ember and said it was neater than his flies deserved. He also said letters from the north come the way geese do, none for weeks and then a skyful.

volumes.title: July: The Pencil Box
volumes.text:
July, and Tolly the ferryman was right: two letters from Da came on one morning, tied together with tarred string. The Curlew is loading dried fish at a place called Skerry Sound, where it does not get dark at all. I read them both twice on the workshop step.

I am Tansy Wickett, and I am making a box every month this year with my great-aunt Lovage in Thimble Yard. July’s is a pencil box for my friend Pip Larkin, who goes away to school in the Lowlands in autumn.

It has my first dovetails. Those are the corner joints shaped like a row of birds’ tails, which lock so the box cannot pull apart. Mine have gaps. Aunt Lovage says they look like my teeth did at seven and will improve the same way. Pip says he will tell the Lowland boys the gaps are for ventilation.

volumes.title: August: The Letter Box
volumes.text:
August. The rule in my great-aunt Lovage’s workshop is that I make one small box a month and give it away. This month I asked to keep one. I am Tansy Wickett, and my Da is a year at sea on the ketch Curlew, and his letters were living under my pillow, getting creased.

Aunt Lovage thought about it while she swept. Then she said the box would be for the letters, and the letters were Da’s, and I would only be minding both. That is how she gets round her own rules. She calls it joinery.

So it is oak, long and shallow, dovetailed with smaller gaps than July’s, with a brass catch that clicks. I lined it with blue paper from the stationer’s. Seven letters fit, lying flat, with room for as many again. I checked that part on purpose. It was the only checking I enjoyed.

volumes.title: September: The Money Box
volumes.text:
September. The bell-ringers of Emberwick are collecting for a new rope, and they asked my great-aunt Lovage for a money box, and she pointed at me with her pencil. I am Tansy Wickett, eleven, her apprentice for this year, a box each month.

A money box is a strange job, because you build a box and then shut it for good. There is a slot in the top and no lid at all. I was pleased with that until Aunt asked how the ringers would ever get their pennies out, short of an axe.

So the bottom slides, but only if you first push one particular corner peg, which looks like all the others. I am not saying which. The ringers shook the box for ten minutes and gave up, and the Tower Captain had to be told privately. It rattles already. I put the first penny in myself.

volumes.title: October: The Candle Box
volumes.text:
October, with gales. This month’s box went the farthest of any: out along the cliff road to the lighthouse on the Grey Coast, for Mrs. Skerrit the keeper, who wanted her spare candles kept dry. I am Tansy Wickett, and I have made ten boxes this year in my great-aunt Lovage’s workshop in Emberwick.

It is long and plain, in elm, with a lid that slides and a thumb-notch to push it by. Aunt Lovage walked out with me to deliver it, both of us leaning into the wind like a pair of ladders.

Mrs. Skerrit writes down every ship that passes. I asked, not very casually, about a ketch called the Curlew, with my Da aboard. She ran her finger down the page. Not yet, she said, but she would look out specially, and she stood a candle from my box in the seaward window.

volumes.title: November: The Box Within
volumes.text:
November. Great-aunt Lovage has a birthday this month, which she denies. I am Tansy Wickett, in my eleventh month of making boxes in her workshop in Thimble Yard, and I built hers in secret, on the afternoons she goes to market.

It looks like a plain walnut box for hairpins. But the floor is not the real floor. Press the back edge and it tips, and underneath is a second space, just deep enough for a folded paper. I put one in. It says, Thank you for the year, in my best writing.

Aunt found the secret in under a minute. I know because I was watching round the door. She took an hour to mention it, and then she only said the hinge was well hung. A letter has come as well. The Curlew is homeward bound, and Da hopes to be in the Ember before midwinter.

volumes.title: December: The Sea Chest
volumes.text:
December, the twelfth box. I am Tansy Wickett. I came to my great-aunt Lovage in Thimble Yard in January, when my Da sailed north on the Curlew, and I have made a box every month since. The last is a sea chest, though only as long as my arm: oak, dovetailed without one gap, with rope handles I spliced myself.

The Curlew came up the Ember on the evening tide on the nineteenth. Mrs. Skerrit at the lighthouse sent word ahead, so I was on the quay with the chest in a wheelbarrow. Da is thinner and has a beard. He opened the lid there on the stones.

Inside I had put one shaving from each of the other eleven boxes, pine to walnut. He looked at them a long time. He is ashore until spring. Aunt Lovage has already put out the wood for January.

volumes.title: The Nail by the Door
volumes.text:
Pinned to the nail by the door of Strake’s boatshed, Saltings Hard, at the mouth of the Ember.

Eli. Abel Reedy, the marsh postman, has ordered a skiff to carry the letters round the creeks. It is the first proper order this shed has had since Father died, and it needs both of us, so I propose terms. I work the mornings. You work the afternoons. Whatever must be said goes on this nail. We have not spoken for nine years and I see no reason to spoil it over one boat. I have chalked her lines on the floor. Do not walk on them. Dorcas.

Dorcas. Agreed. I walked round your lines and they are fair ones, though she looks wide to me. I have picked out the oak for her keel and stood it by the bench. Your handwriting has not improved in nine years. Eli.

volumes.title: Keel and Complaints
volumes.text:
Two notes from the nail in Strake’s boatshed, where a sister and brother are building a skiff for the marsh postman without speaking to one another.

Eli. The keel is laid and it is straight. I sighted along it at first light with the gulls for company. I have set up the stem at the bow end and wedged it true. My mallet was not on its hook this morning. It was on the windowsill. Things have hooks for a reason. Dorcas.

Dorcas. The mallet was on the sill because the hook is where you hung your wet oilskin. I fitted the sternpost this afternoon and she has a backbone now, bow to stern. You can stand at one end and see a boat that is not there yet. Father used to say that was the best day. Also you leave shavings in the glue pot. Eli.

volumes.title: Moulds and Manners
volumes.text:
Dorcas. Nailed up in Strake’s shed at the end of my afternoon, since notes are all we exchange. I set the moulds along the keel of the postman’s skiff today, the board shapes that show where her planks will run. She has more belly than your chalk lines gave her. I looked twice. Did you think I would not notice? Eli.

Eli. She has more belly because Abel Reedy carries parcels as well as letters, and at midwinter a goose for every farm on the marsh. A narrow boat full of geese is a short story. I widened her amidships and would do it again. You may tell me I am wrong in writing. Bar the doors properly when you leave tonight. The tides are making, and you know why I ask. Dorcas.

Dorcas. I know why. I barred them. I always do, square in both brackets. Eli.

volumes.title: The First Plank
volumes.text:
Eli. For the nail by the door, there being no other way we talk. The first plank of Reedy’s skiff is on, the one that lies against the keel. It is larch, long as the shed, and it has to twist like a ribbon between bow and stern. I held one end with clamps, the middle with my knee and the far end with strong language. It took the whole morning. Dorcas.

Dorcas. I hung its partner on the other side this afternoon. It took me till dark, and I used your language and some of my own. Father and the two of us used to hang a plank in an hour. Two people could still. I mention it as arithmetic. Eli.

Eli. Two people would need a conversation first. I have left you the good clamps, the ones Father marked with a red stripe. Dorcas.

volumes.title: Steam and Larch
volumes.text:
Dorcas. Pinned up at Strake’s shed, Saltings Hard, with my left hand. I lit the steam box at noon. Larch will not take the bend at the skiff’s bow cold, so each plank cooks in the long wooden chest over the boiler until it droops like a wet towel, and then you run. You have about as long as it takes to say the alphabet. I got the plank on. I also got my thumb on the boiler lid. Eli.

Eli. Four planks a side now and they lie sweetly; I looked along them at first light. There is a pot of salve on this nail. It is Mother’s, goose fat and marigold. No note goes with it. Dorcas.

Dorcas. Found a pot. Used it. Not thanking anyone in particular. The postman’s boat is coming on. Eli.

volumes.title: About the Petrel
volumes.text:
Two notes from the nail in Strake’s boatshed, with the postman’s skiff half planked.

Dorcas. Nine years is long enough to say this on paper. The night the flood tide floated Father’s last boat, the Petrel, off her stocks and out to sea, I shut the shed. I dropped the bar across the big doors, square in both brackets, and left by the side door. You were in here after me. I have always supposed you lifted it to look at the tide. Eli.

Eli. I have read your note four times. I came back that night for my spectacles and never touched the bar. It was down, I grant you, but you always dropped it short at the seaward end, and I have supposed the water found that out. So each of us has been sure of the other. The seventh plank is ready for you. Dorcas.

volumes.title: Rivets by Lamplight
volumes.text:
Left on the nail, Strake’s boatshed, Saltings Hard. The Strakes have not spoken in nine years and are building a skiff by turns.

Eli. The planks must be riveted now, copper nails through each overlap, and it cannot be done alone. One of us holds a heavy iron against the nail head outside the hull while the other hammers the point over on the inside. I have tried it with a sandbag and a broom. Come at six. We need not talk. One knock on the planking means ready, two means next. Dorcas.

Dorcas. I came at six, as you know, since you were four feet away with a plank between us. Three hundred rivets by lamplight and not one word. You knock exactly as you used to on my bedroom wall. I had forgotten that. Same time tomorrow. Eli.

volumes.title: Ribs and Rain
volumes.text:
Notes from the nail by the door of Strake’s shed, where Dorcas and Eli Strake are building a skiff for Abel Reedy, the marsh postman.

Dorcas. Rain on the roof all day, which is good weather for bending ribs. Thin oak, steamed soft, pressed down into the hull and riveted before it changes its mind. We did eleven together this evening, still not speaking. Reedy called in to look. He said to tell my sister the boat is handsome. Consider yourself told. Eli.

Eli. He stood between us for half an hour and carried remarks from one to the other like a man passing plates. On his way out he said he has delivered letters for forty years and never before seen two people post them four feet. I did not laugh until he had gone. The last ribs go in tomorrow. Bring the short hammer. Dorcas.

volumes.title: Seats and Second Thoughts
volumes.text:
On the nail, Strake’s boatshed, Saltings Hard. A sister and brother who share the shed but not a word are fitting out the postman’s skiff.

Eli. The seats went in this morning, three of them, each braced to her sides with a knee of crooked oak that grew in that shape in a Lowland hedge. She is stiff as a basket now. I see you have built a locker under the stern seat for the mailbag, with a lid that sheds water and a little rack inside for the letters that must not be bent. It is good work. I have looked at it twice. Dorcas.

Dorcas. You looked three times. There are three sets of bootprints in the sawdust. Thank you. I did not think I would write that this year. I have rounded the edges of your seats, for Reedy’s knees. Eli.

volumes.title: The Rotten Bracket
volumes.text:
Two notes from the nail in Strake’s boatshed, Saltings Hard, written the week the doors were readied for the launch.

Eli. I took down the old iron brackets that hold the door bar, to swing the doors wide for her. The seaward one came away in my hand. The bolts behind it are rusted to threads and the post is soft as cheese, old rot, older than nine years. A child could have pushed that bar out. A flood tide certainly could. It never held, however it was dropped. It was not you. Dorcas.

Dorcas. I went to look, and stood some time. Nor you. I dropped that bar square the night the Petrel went, and you never touched it, and the sea lifted it out regardless. Father fitted that bracket and never would be told about it. Nine years. I will bring new oak for the post tomorrow. Eli.

volumes.title: Paint and a Name
volumes.text:
Dorcas. For the nail in Strake’s shed, in the last week of the postman’s skiff. Second coat is on: grey-green, the colour of the marsh in the morning, with a white line at her rail so Reedy can be seen in a mist. He says the builders are to name her. I thought Petrel, after Father’s boat that was lost from here. Eli.

Eli. No. That boat has had nine years of us already. This one was built by two people passing notes on a nail, for a man who carries letters. I have painted a name on a spare board for you to see. It says Reply. Dorcas.

Dorcas. Reply. Yes. I will cut the letters into her stern myself. I would like to come in the morning tomorrow, on your tide, if the morning will have me. Eli.

volumes.title: Launch on the Morning Tide
volumes.text:
The last note on the nail in Strake’s boatshed, Saltings Hard, in two hands on a single sheet.

We launched the Reply this morning on the top of the tide, the two of us on the ropes, and she slid down the hard and sat on the water like a gull. Abel Reedy stepped in with the mailbag, stowed it in its locker, and rowed off up the creek with the first post she ever carried. She does not leak a drop. Dorcas.

For the record, the first words spoken between the Strakes in nine years were “Mind your end,” and “Mind your own.” After that it came easier. We have talked since about the price of larch, and about Father, and about who is to have the mornings. Shed barred, new bracket holds. Gone to breakfast, both of us. Eli.
